_about: Each state's sales tax rate (percent) and what's different for restaurants. meals / alcohol: {"rate": R} replaces the state rate on prepared food / drinks served (local taxes still added, unless "noLocal"), {"add": A} adds to the total. notes: local restaurant taxes not in the rate (the store checks its own). Checked October 2026 against the sources named.

notes: No state sales tax; many boroughs and cities have their own (in the rate), and some add alcohol or bed taxes.
Arizona cities tax restaurants and bars at their own rate (the rate here is for restaurants where the city publishes one).
Many cities add an advertising and promotion (hotel and restaurant) tax on prepared food, usually 1 to 3%.
Mixed drinks served: a 4% mixed drink tax and a 10% supplemental tax.
Home-rule cities collect their own sales tax: register with the city as well.

CT.source: CT DRS PS 2019(5): meals 7.35% since October 1, 2019

DC.source: DC OTR: general 6% through September 30, 2027 (the increase to 7% postponed); restaurant meals and drinks 10%

notes: Miami-Dade County: a food and beverage tax (up to 2%) at restaurants licensed to serve alcohol.
The general excise tax is on the business; it may be passed on to guests at up to 4.712% (with the county's 0.5%).
Resort cities (Ketchum, Sun Valley, McCall and others) add a local option tax, up to 3%.
Chicago adds a 0.5% restaurant tax, and 1% more in the Metropolitan Pier and Exposition area; other cities have their own.
Many counties and cities add a food and beverage tax, usually 1 to 2%.
Some cities add a restaurant tax, up to 3%.

ME.source: Maine Revenue Services: prepared food and liquor served 8%

MD.source: Comptroller of Maryland: alcoholic beverages 9% since July 1, 2011

notes: Most cities and towns (Boston among them) add a 0.75% local meals tax: 7% in all.
Minneapolis and some other cities add a food and beverage tax (downtown Minneapolis 3%).
Many cities add a tourism tax on restaurants, usually 1 to 3%.
Resort towns (Whitefish, Big Sky, West Yellowstone and others) add a resort tax, up to 4%.
Some cities add an occupation tax on restaurants (Omaha 2.5%).

NH.source: NH meals and rooms tax 8.5% since October 1, 2021 (a 2026 bill to raise it failed)

notes: Urban Enterprise Zones may charge half the rate; Atlantic City adds a luxury tax on drinks.
Gross receipts tax: on the business, usually passed on to guests.
Some counties add a 1% prepared food and beverage tax (Mecklenburg, Wake, Durham, Dare and others).
Some cities add a restaurant and lodging tax (Bismarck, Fargo and others).
Ashland adds a 5% food and beverage tax.
Allegheny County adds a 7% drink tax on poured drinks; Philadelphia a 10% liquor tax on drinks.

RI.source: RI Division of Taxation: 1% local meals and beverage tax

notes: Many cities and counties add a local hospitality tax on prepared food, up to 2%.
Many cities add a municipal gross receipts tax on restaurants, up to 1%. The state rate goes back to 4.5% on July 1, 2027.

TN.source: TN Department of Revenue: liquor-by-the-drink tax 15%, on top of sales tax

TX.source: Texas Comptroller: mixed beverage sales tax 8.25% on drinks served, instead of sales tax

notes: Most counties add a 1% restaurant tax.
Some towns add a 1% local option meals and alcohol tax.
VT.source: Vermont Department of Taxes: meals 9%, alcohol served 10%

notes: Most counties and cities add a local meals tax, usually 4 to 7.5%.
Spirits served are taxed by the liter as well.
Some cities add a food and beverage tax; premier resort areas a resort tax.
